summary: The paper trains a Qwen3-14B shell agent with A³, a GRPO-family RL method. A³ builds turn-level advantages from episode-relative reward, AST-based similarity of shell command sub-chains, and tree-level trajectory margins. It adds σ-Reveal, an inference-time heuristic that picks a token-budgeted subset of the initial file tree to show the agent. The authors also build ShellOps/ShellOps-Pro, a verifiable dataset of filesystem lookup, aggregate and edit tasks. A³ is the best 14B method on most streams, with its largest margins on the authors' own ShellOps.

claims.claim: A³ is the strongest Qwen3-14B method across the mixed benchmark
claims.evidence: Table 1 exact match: large gains on ShellOps (string 46.5 vs best baseline 27.5; hybrid 21.9 vs 11.3) and AB-DB (23.6 vs 15.1). Margins are small elsewhere: AB-OS 58.6 vs ReAct 57.9 (GSPO 61.4 is higher), TableBench 30.7 vs 25.0. In Table 2 Pass@3/5, untrained ReAct beats A³ on AB-OS (79.7/86.2 vs 76.2/79.3) and RetroAgent beats it on EHRCon. Single runs, no variance.

claims.claim: σ-Reveal improves results by selecting token-budgeted workspace context
claims.evidence: Table 1: gains of 0.7-3.8 pts on most streams (e.g. ShellOps string 46.5→48.5, hybrid 21.9→24.6), but small regressions on Files AB-DB (46.6→46.4) and Files ShellOps (26.5→25.7). No variance, so most deltas are within plausible noise.

claims.claim: A³ reaches the Qwen3-235B range on ShellOps-Pro at longer horizons; gap remains to Kimi-K2.6/GLM-5.1
claims.evidence: §4.4 and the ShellOps-Pro table (H_max 6/8/10): 150 OOD tasks, authors' own dataset.

claims.claim: Advantage computation stays at standard GRPO cost
claims.evidence: Table 5 efficiency comparison; App. E AST similarity cost.

patterns.note: RL credit assignment for CLI agents improves a 14B policy, mainly on the authors' dataset; single model, no variance.
σ-Reveal ranks files lexically (name matches task tokens, depth prior, extension prior); gains are small and inconsistent.
Token-budgeted initial context selection (subtree-closed knapsack under budget B).
Shell commands as the native action space.
Sandboxed execution with 10 s timeout (App. B.2).

methodology.sample: 6 benchmark streams (AgentBench OS/DB, DataBench, EHRCon, TableBench, ShellOps 714 in-distribution tasks) + ShellOps-Pro 150 OOD tasks; 30% of the training split used
methodology.baselines: ReAct, LATS, rStar, GSPO, GiGPO, HGPO, RetroAgent on Qwen3-14B under the same config; Kimi-K2.6, GLM-5.1, Qwen3-235B as frontier inference
methodology.models: Qwen3-14B policy only; Qwen3-8B as secondary LLM judge; Claude Opus 4.7 for data label audits
methodology.ablations: A³ branch ablation and window length (Table 4); channel contribution shares (Fig. 4a)
methodology.contamination_controls: Instances judged hallucinatory/mislabeled by Claude audits excluded; no training-data overlap check
methodology.languages: Bash over mixed-file workspaces; horizon 6 steps (up to 10 on ShellOps-Pro)

standards.artifacts: Code at github.com/Hoyant-Su/Agentic-RL-A3; dataset release not explicitly confirmed

biases.detail: The largest gains are on ShellOps, a dataset built by the same authors, with labels from Claude audits.
Qwen3-14B is the only trained policy.
Single runs for an RL method; several margins are 1-3 pts.
6-step horizon and 10 s sandbox timeout; tasks are file lookup/aggregation/edit, not software builds.
Secondary LLM-judge metric (Qwen3-8B) and Claude-generated labels are not validated against humans.

coi.affiliations: Fudan University, Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai Innovation Institute
coi.detail: Academic authors with no vendor tie. The authors both built the ShellOps benchmark and propose the method that tops it, which is a self-evaluation risk rather than a commercial conflict.

verdict_reason: Several RL baselines run under matched configs, plus a component ablation and released code. But it uses a single model with no variance, the largest wins are on the authors' own dataset, the horizons are short, and σ-Reveal's gains are small and inconsistent.
applicability: Weak transfer. The team will use frontier agents on hosts it does not train, so A³ itself is irrelevant. σ-Reveal is a reusable harness idea: pre-select a token-budgeted, directory-preserving slice of the file tree using name, depth and extension heuristics before the first action. It is cheap to try across several repositories, but its evidence here is small, noisy gains on shallow-horizon tasks. Repo maps or deterministic grep/LSP retrieval would need their own A/B on the team's Java repos before adoption. The paper offers no evidence on spec-driven development or multi-host consistency.
